title: Pest or Disease? How to Tell What Is Wrong With Your Crop
metaTitle: Pest or Disease? How to Tell What Is Hurting Your Crop
metaDescription: Pest or disease? Learn the signs that separate insect damage from fungal, bacterial and virus disease, the quick field tests, and when it is both.
excerpt: To tell a pest or disease apart, look for the culprit first. Chewed or cut tissue, holes, droppings, eggs and the insects themselves point to a pest, while spots with borders, ooze, mold, rot or mottled leaves with no insect in sight point to a disease. Yellowing with no spots can also come from the soil or the water. With anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, the free Pest Finder and Disease Finder sort the signs, and Anee, its smart farm technician, can read a photo when you are still unsure.

blocks.text:
The answer decides what you buy. An insecticide does nothing for a fungus, and no spray at all cures a virus. IRRI's Rice Knowledge Bank puts the average loss of rice to pests and diseases at an estimated 37 percent of the crop each year. It also says that timely, accurate diagnosis can cut those losses.

Not every sick plant has a pest or a disease, either. IRRI notes that crop problems also come from wind, water, temperature and soil acidity. So keep a third answer in mind: the soil, the water or the weather.

items: Look for the culprit first: insects, eggs, droppings and chewed tissue mean a pest.
Spots with borders, ooze, mold, rot and mottling with no insect in sight mean a disease.
Even yellowing over a whole field with no spots often comes from nutrients or water.
Some diseases ride on insects, like tungro on the green leafhopper, so it can be both.
Never spray just to find out. Diagnose first, then pick the product.

blocks.text:
Some diseases ride on pests. Tungro is a virus disease, but leafhoppers carry it from plant to plant, and the green leafhopper is the most efficient one. IRRI says spraying the leafhoppers often fails, because they keep moving in from nearby fields. Prevention works better: resistant varieties, planting at the same time as your neighbors, and plowing infected stubble after harvest.

The brown planthopper does the same with [rice grassy stunt](/diseases/rice-grassy-stunt). In both cases the plant shows a disease, but the cause walks in on legs. That is why the finders and Anee ask about insects even when you report yellow leaves.
Five field checks before you decide

items.title: Read the pattern
items.text: Step back first. Patches that grow outward, rows, field edges or the whole field each point somewhere different. A problem along one side may follow water, wind or a neighbor's spray.

items.title: Look under the leaves and at the base
items.text: Go in the early morning, when many pests are still on the plant. Turn the leaves over and part the hill to see the base.

items.title: Pull a tiller
items.text: A stem borer deadheart pulls out easily. Kresek, the seedling wilt of bacterial leaf blight, does not, IRRI notes.

items.title: Do the ooze test
items.text: Squeeze the base of a wilted seedling, or cut a young streak and stand the leaf in a clear glass of water. Yellowish ooze or a cloudy stream from the cut end points to bacteria.

items.title: Check your records
items.text: Note the growth stage, the last fertilizer and the recent weather. IRRI warns that tungro can look like nitrogen or zinc deficiency or water stress, so your records help rule those out.

blocks.title: Do not spray to find out
blocks.text: Spraying an insecticide to see if the problem stops wastes money and kills the spiders and wasps that protect your crop. Diagnose first. Then, if you need a product, use one registered with the FPA for your crop and follow its label.

blocks.text: Questions about telling a pest from a disease

items.q: What are the signs of a pest?
items.a: Holes, chewed or cut leaves, droppings, eggs and the insects themselves. Some pests suck sap instead and leave yellow or dry patches, so look at the base of the plant too.

items.q: What are the signs of a disease?
items.a: Spots with borders or halos, streaks, ooze, mold, rot, wilting, and mottled or stunted plants with no insect in sight. Fungi, bacteria and viruses each leave their own marks.

items.q: Can a virus be sprayed away?
items.a: No. IRRI says a rice plant infected by tungro cannot be cured. Prevention works instead: resistant varieties, synchronous planting and plowing infected stubble after harvest.

items.q: What if I still cannot tell pest or disease?
items.a: Use both finders, send a photo to Anee, or ask your municipal agriculturist. Do not spray to test, since the wrong product costs money and kills the natural enemies of pests.

items.q: Can weather damage look like disease?
items.a: Yes. IRRI lists wind, water, temperature and soil acidity among the non living causes of crop problems. Check the weather and your water before you blame a pest or a disease.
